meta_desc: IB DP Chemistry practice covering S2.1 The ionic model, guide topic S2.1.
final_note: You worked through S2.1 The ionic model — 3 guide statements.

concepts.def: A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons so that it has more protons than electrons. Metal atoms form cations: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. The charge on an ion equals (number of protons − number of electrons).

A negatively charged ion, formed when an atom gains one or more electrons so that it has more electrons than protons. Non-metal atoms form anions: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻, O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻. The nucleus, and so the number of protons, is unchanged when any ion forms.

concepts.term: Predicting the charge of an ion from electron configuration
concepts.def: For the metals of groups 1 and 2, aluminium, and the non-metals of groups 15 to 17, an atom in a simple ionic compound loses or gains the number of electrons that gives it the electron configuration of the nearest noble gas. The metals of groups 1 and 2, and aluminium, lose all their outer (valence) electrons: Na 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ → Na⁺ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Al [Ne] 3s² 3p¹ → Al³⁺ [Ne]. In their ionic compounds, the non-metals of groups 15 to 17 gain the electrons needed to complete their outer s and p sublevels, so the charge is −(8 − number of outer electrons): O 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ → O²⁻ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; S [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ → S²⁻ [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶; N 1s² 2s² 2p³ → N³⁻ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.

concepts.term: Ions of transition elements with different charges
concepts.def: A transition element can form ions of more than one charge. When a first-row transition element forms an ion, its 4s electrons are removed before its 3d electrons. Iron, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², forms Fe²⁺, [Ar] 3d⁶ (both 4s electrons lost), and Fe³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁵ (both 4s electrons and one 3d electron lost). Copper, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, forms Cu⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰, and Cu²⁺, [Ar] 3d⁹. The charge is shown in the name by a Roman numeral: iron(II), iron(III), copper(I), copper(II).

The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. The attraction is non-directional: in a lattice each ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it, not to one partner. In sodium chloride each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions, and each Cl⁻ ion by six Na⁺ ions, and every one of these attractions is the same ionic bond. Electron transfer is how the ions can be formed; it is not the bond itself.

concepts.term: Deducing the formula of an ionic compound
concepts.def: The ions are combined in the simplest ratio that makes the total charge zero, with the cation written first. Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ give MgCl₂; Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃ (2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0). A polyatomic ion is kept intact as a unit, and brackets are placed round it when more than one is needed: Mg²⁺ and OH⁻ give Mg(OH)₂; NH₄⁺ and SO₄²⁻ give (NH₄)₂SO₄.

A binary ionic compound contains ions of two elements. It is named with the cation first, using the name of the metal, followed by the anion, whose name takes the suffix "-ide": sodium chloride NaCl, magnesium oxide MgO, calcium nitride Ca₃N₂, aluminium sulfide Al₂S₃. Greek number prefixes (di-, tri-), used for covalent compounds such as sulfur trioxide, are not used in these names. For a metal that forms ions of more than one charge, a Roman numeral gives the charge of the cation: Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide, Cu₂O is copper(I) oxide, CuCl₂ is copper(II) chloride.

An ion made of two or more covalently bonded atoms that carries an overall charge and stays intact as a unit in ionic compounds. The seven to be known by name and formula are: ammonium NH₄⁺, hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻ and phosphate PO₄³⁻. Ammonium is the only cation among them. Compounds are named from the ions: Na₂CO₃ sodium carbonate, NaHCO₃ sodium hydrogencarbonate, Ca(NO₃)₂ calcium nitrate, (NH₄)₃PO₄ ammonium phosphate.

The three-dimensional structure of a solid ionic compound: a regular, repeating arrangement of cations and anions that extends throughout the crystal, with each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge. There are no molecules in an ionic lattice, so a crystal contains an enormous and variable number of ions.

concepts.term: Empirical formula of an ionic compound
concepts.def: The formula of an ionic compound is an empirical formula: it gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions in the lattice, not a molecule. MgCl₂ means one Mg²⁺ ion for every two Cl⁻ ions; Al₂O₃ means two Al³⁺ ions for every three O²⁻ ions. The subscript 2 in MgCl₂ counts chloride ions; there are no Cl₂ molecules in the compound.

Volatility is the tendency of a substance to vaporize. Ionic compounds have low volatility and high melting and boiling points (sodium chloride melts at 801 °C) because to melt or vaporize them the strong electrostatic attractions between each ion and the many oppositely charged ions around it must be overcome, and this requires a large amount of energy.

An electric current needs mobile charged particles. In a solid ionic compound the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so the solid does not conduct. When the compound is molten or dissolved in water (aqueous), the ions are free to move, and the compound conducts: cations move towards the negative electrode and anions towards the positive electrode. The charge is carried through the melt or solution by ions, not by free electrons.

Many ionic compounds dissolve in water, which is a polar solvent: the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules are attracted to cations and the partially positive hydrogen atoms to anions, so the ions separate from the lattice and become surrounded by water molecules. Ionic compounds are generally insoluble in non-polar solvents such as hexane, whose molecules are not attracted strongly enough to the ions. Not every ionic compound is soluble in water: calcium carbonate and barium sulfate, for example, are insoluble.

The standard enthalpy change that occurs on the formation of gaseous ions from one mole of the solid lattice, for example NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g). Units: kJ mol⁻¹. Separating ions that attract each other requires energy, so lattice enthalpies are positive (endothermic). The larger the lattice enthalpy, the stronger the ionic bonding in the compound.

concepts.term: Effect of ion charge and ion radius on lattice enthalpy
concepts.def: Lattice enthalpy increases as the charges on the ions increase and as the ionic radii decrease, because the electrostatic attraction between two ions is greater when their charges are larger and their centres are closer. Magnesium oxide (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻) has a far larger lattice enthalpy than sodium chloride (Na⁺ and Cl⁻). Among compounds of singly charged ions, the lattice enthalpy decreases in the order NaF > NaCl > KCl as the ions get larger.

mcqs.q: An atom of element X has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. Which ion does X form in its ionic compounds?
options: X²⁺
X⁶⁺
X²⁻
X⁶⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
mcqs.explain: X has six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). It gains two electrons, giving 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, and with 16 protons and 18 electrons its charge is 2−. (X is sulfur, which forms S²⁻, as in sodium sulfide, Na₂S.)
rationales: Gaining two electrons does give X a complete 3p sublevel, but electrons are negative: 16 protons and 18 electrons give a charge of 16 − 18 = −2, not +2.

Losing all six outer electrons would leave the full shell 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, but having a full shell does not make an ion form. Removing six electrons would need a very large amount of energy; a non-metal atom with a nearly complete outer sublevel gains two electrons instead.

X has six outer electrons (3s² 3p⁴). It gains two electrons, giving 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, and with 16 protons and 18 electrons its charge is 2−. (X is sulfur, which forms S²⁻, as in sodium sulfide, Na₂S.)

The charge is not the number of outer electrons. X needs only two more electrons to complete its 3p sublevel, so it gains two and forms X²⁻ (the argon configuration). Gaining six electrons would carry it four electrons beyond the argon configuration.

mcqs.q: Copper (atomic number 29) forms both Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ ions. Which describes how a copper atom forms a Cu²⁺ ion?
options: It loses the two electrons from its 4s sublevel.
It loses two 3d electrons and keeps its 4s one.
Its nucleus gains two protons; its electrons stay.
It loses its one 4s electron and one 3d electron.
mcqs.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
mcqs.explain: Copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. The 4s electron is removed first, then one 3d electron, giving Cu²⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁹. Losing only the 4s electron gives Cu⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰.
rationales: Copper has only one 4s electron: its configuration is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, one of the exceptions to the Aufbau order. After the 4s electron, the second electron must come from 3d.
Electrons are not removed in the reverse of the filling order. The 4s electron of a first-row transition element is removed before any 3d electron, so Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹ with no 4s electron.
Forming an ion never changes the number of protons: two extra protons would make the atom a different element (gallium). Cu²⁺ has 29 protons and 27 electrons.
Copper is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. The 4s electron is removed first, then one 3d electron, giving Cu²⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁹. Losing only the 4s electron gives Cu⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰.

mcqs.q: An iron atom has the electron configuration [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Iron forms a sulfate with the formula Fe₂(SO₄)₃. What is the electron configuration of the iron ion in this compound? (4s⁰ shows that the 4s sublevel is empty.)
options: [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s⁰
[Ar] 3d⁵ 4s⁰
[Ar] 3d³ 4s²
[Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²
mcqs.specStatementText: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
mcqs.explain: Three sulfate ions carry 3 × (−2) = −6, so the two iron ions carry +6 and each is Fe³⁺. Iron loses its two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron: [Ar] 3d⁵.
rationales: This is Fe²⁺, read from the subscript 2 on Fe. Subscripts count ions: two iron ions must balance three SO₄²⁻ ions (total −6), so each iron ion is Fe³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁵.
Three sulfate ions carry 3 × (−2) = −6, so the two iron ions carry +6 and each is Fe³⁺. Iron loses its two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron: [Ar] 3d⁵.
The charge, 3+, is right, but the electrons have been taken from 3d while 4s is kept. When iron forms an ion its 4s electrons are removed first, so Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
This is the configuration of the iron atom. The ion's charge comes from losing electrons, not from any change in the nucleus, so Fe³⁺ has three fewer electrons than the atom: [Ar] 3d⁵.

mcqs.q: Which describes the ionic bonding in solid sodium chloride?
options: Attraction between oppositely charged ions in all directions
Transfer of one electron from each sodium atom to a chlorine atom
Attraction joining each Na⁺ to one Cl⁻ in an NaCl molecule
A pair of electrons shared unequally by Na and Cl atoms
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It is non-directional: each Na⁺ ion attracts all the Cl⁻ ions around it in the lattice, and each Cl⁻ ion attracts all the Na⁺ ions around it.
rationales: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It is non-directional: each Na⁺ ion attracts all the Cl⁻ ions around it in the lattice, and each Cl⁻ ion attracts all the Na⁺ ions around it.
Electron transfer is one way the ions can be formed, but it is an event, not the bond. The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that exist in the lattice.
Sodium chloride contains no molecules. It is a giant lattice in which each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by, and attracted to, six Cl⁻ ions; NaCl gives the 1 : 1 ratio of the ions.
A shared electron pair is a covalent bond. In sodium chloride the electron has been transferred, and the particles are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held by electrostatic attraction.

mcqs.q: A sample of sodium chloride is made by burning sodium in chlorine. In the solid, each Na⁺ ion has six Cl⁻ ions as its nearest neighbours, all at the same distance. Which statement about the bonding of one Na⁺ ion is correct?
options: It is bonded only to the Cl⁻ ion that accepted its electron.
It forms one bond, as its atom had one electron to give.
It is bonded to all six Cl⁻ ions by shared electron pairs.
It is bonded to all six Cl⁻ ions, attracting each of them equally.
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It depends only on the charges and the distance between the ions, and all six Cl⁻ ions are at the same distance, so the Na⁺ ion is bonded equally to all six.
rationales: Ions carry no record of where their electrons went. The attraction to the Cl⁻ ion that happened to take the electron is exactly the same as the attraction to the other five, so all six are ionic bonds.
An ion does not form a fixed number of bonds set by the electrons its atom lost. Each ion is attracted to every oppositely charged ion around it; the Na⁺ ion here forms six equivalent ionic bonds.
Six neighbours is right, but there are no shared electron pairs: shared pairs are covalent bonds. The Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held by electrostatic attraction between opposite charges.

The ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. It depends only on the charges and the distance between the ions, and all six Cl⁻ ions are at the same distance, so the Na⁺ ion is bonded equally to all six.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of sodium phosphate, with a correct reason?
options: Na₃PO₄, as three Na⁺ ions balance one PO₄³⁻ ion
Na₂PO₄, as phosphate has a 2− charge, like sulfate
NaPO₄, as one sodium ion pairs with one phosphate ion
Na(PO₄)₃, as each ion's charge is its own subscript
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: Sodium forms Na⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Three Na⁺ ions (+3) balance one PO₄³⁻ ion (−3). Only one phosphate ion is needed, so no brackets are used: Na₃PO₄.
rationales: Sodium forms Na⁺ and phosphate is PO₄³⁻. Three Na⁺ ions (+3) balance one PO₄³⁻ ion (−3). Only one phosphate ion is needed, so no brackets are used: Na₃PO₄.
Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, not PO₄²⁻: the -ate ending does not fix the charge. With PO₄³⁻, three Na⁺ ions are needed: Na₃PO₄.
One Na⁺ (+1) and one PO₄³⁻ (−3) give a total charge of −2, so NaPO₄ is not neutral. Three Na⁺ ions are needed: Na₃PO₄.
Subscripts count ions; they are not each ion's own charge. Na(PO₄)₃ would carry +1 + 3 × (−3) = −8. Three Na⁺ ions balance one PO₄³⁻ ion: Na₃PO₄.

mcqs.q: Which formula is paired with its correct name?
options: Cu₂O, copper(II) oxide
Fe₂O₃, iron trioxide
CuO, copper(II) oxide
CaS, calcium sulfur
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: One O²⁻ ion (−2) is balanced by one copper ion, so the copper ion is Cu²⁺ and the Roman numeral is (II).
rationales: The subscript 2 counts copper ions; it is not their charge. Two copper ions balance one O²⁻ ion (−2), so each is Cu⁺: Cu₂O is copper(I) oxide.

'Iron trioxide' would mean one iron to three oxygens, which is not the ratio in Fe₂O₃. Number prefixes are the convention for covalent compounds such as sulfur trioxide; an ionic compound is named from its ions, with a Roman numeral for the charge of the iron ion.
One O²⁻ ion (−2) is balanced by one copper ion, so the copper ion is Cu²⁺ and the Roman numeral is (II).
The anion is the sulfide ion, S²⁻. The anion of a binary ionic compound takes the suffix -ide: CaS is calcium sulfide.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct formula, including its charge, of a polyatomic ion in aqueous solution?
options: NH₄⁻(aq)
OH⁻(aq)
NO₃²⁻(aq)
HCO₃²⁻(aq)
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: The hydroxide ion is OH⁻. The correct formulas of the other three ions are NH₄⁺ (ammonium), NO₃⁻ (nitrate) and HCO₃⁻ (hydrogencarbonate).
rationales: Ammonium is the one positive polyatomic ion: NH₄⁺, formed when ammonia accepts H⁺. In its compounds it takes the place of a metal cation, as in NH₄Cl.
The hydroxide ion is OH⁻. The correct formulas of the other three ions are NH₄⁺ (ammonium), NO₃⁻ (nitrate) and HCO₃⁻ (hydrogencarbonate).
Not every -ate ion is 2−. Sulfate and carbonate are 2−, but nitrate is NO₃⁻, as in sodium nitrate NaNO₃.
The hydrogen in hydrogencarbonate is present as H⁺ added to CO₃²⁻, which reduces the charge by one: HCO₃⁻, as in sodium hydrogencarbonate NaHCO₃.

mcqs.q: Aluminium, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹, reacts with oxygen, 1s² 2s² 2p⁴, to form aluminium oxide. Which gives its formula with a correct reason?
options: Al₂O₃, as two Al³⁺ ions cancel the charge of three O²⁻
Al₃O₂, as each ion's charge is written as its own subscript
AlO, as each aluminium ion is paired with one oxide ion
Al₂O, as oxygen has six outer electrons and forms O⁶⁻
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: Aluminium loses three electrons to form Al³⁺ and oxygen gains two to form O²⁻. The lowest ratio with zero total charge is 2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0, so the formula is Al₂O₃.
rationales: Aluminium loses three electrons to form Al³⁺ and oxygen gains two to form O²⁻. The lowest ratio with zero total charge is 2 × (+3) + 3 × (−2) = 0, so the formula is Al₂O₃.
Al₃O₂ would have a total charge of 3 × (+3) + 2 × (−2) = +5. The charge of each ion becomes the subscript of the OTHER ion, which gives Al₂O₃.
Al³⁺ + O²⁻ has a total charge of +1, so AlO is not neutral. The ions combine in the ratio that cancels the charges: two Al³⁺ to three O²⁻.
Oxygen does not form O⁶⁻. It needs two electrons to complete its 2p sublevel, so it gains two and forms O²⁻; with Al³⁺ this gives Al₂O₃.

mcqs.q: The formula of magnesium chloride is MgCl₂. What does this formula represent?
options: One molecule of one Mg atom bonded to two Cl atoms
Mg²⁺ ions combined 1 : 1 with chlorine molecules, Cl₂
A Mg atom sharing an electron pair with each Cl atom
The 1 : 2 ratio of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in a lattice
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattices, and their formulas are empirical formulas: MgCl₂ gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions, one Mg²⁺ for every two Cl⁻.
rationales: Magnesium chloride contains no molecules. It is a lattice of Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in which each ion is surrounded by several ions of opposite charge; the formula gives only their ratio.
The subscript 2 counts chloride ions, not atoms in a Cl₂ molecule. The two Cl⁻ ions are separate, each surrounded by Mg²⁺ ions in the lattice.
Shared electron pairs are covalent bonds. Magnesium chloride is ionic: magnesium has lost two electrons to become Mg²⁺, and the ions are held by electrostatic attraction.
Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattices, and their formulas are empirical formulas: MgCl₂ gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the ions, one Mg²⁺ for every two Cl⁻.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride is correct?
options: When molten, it conducts because it releases free electrons.
When molten, it conducts because its ions are free to move.
When solid, it conducts because it is made up of charged ions.
When solid, it has no ions; ions form only when it melts.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: A current needs mobile charged particles. In molten (or aqueous) sodium chloride the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are free to move, so it conducts; in the solid the same ions are fixed in the lattice.
rationales: There are no free electrons in molten sodium chloride. The current is carried by ions: Na⁺ moves towards the negative electrode and Cl⁻ towards the positive electrode.
A current needs mobile charged particles. In molten (or aqueous) sodium chloride the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are free to move, so it conducts; in the solid the same ions are fixed in the lattice.
Solid sodium chloride does not conduct. Its ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice; charged particles carry a current only if they can move.
The ions are already present in the solid lattice. Solid NaCl does not conduct because its ions cannot move, not because it has none; melting only frees the existing ions.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water but not in hexane, C₆H₁₄. Which explanation is correct?
options: Water lowers the melting point of NaCl so that it melts at room temperature.
The ions fit into the spaces between water molecules but not hexane ones.
Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions and separate them from the lattice.
Water turns the neutral NaCl units into ions, which then spread out.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: Water molecules are polar: their partially negative O atoms are attracted to Na⁺ and their partially positive H atoms to Cl⁻, so the ions leave the lattice and are surrounded by water. Hexane is non-polar and is not attracted strongly enough to the ions.
rationales: Dissolving is not melting: NaCl melts at 801 °C. It dissolves at room temperature because water molecules are attracted to the ions and pull them into solution.
Dissolving does not depend on gaps between solvent molecules. It depends on attraction: polar water molecules are attracted to the ions, and non-polar hexane molecules are not.

Water molecules are polar: their partially negative O atoms are attracted to Na⁺ and their partially positive H atoms to Cl⁻, so the ions leave the lattice and are surrounded by water. Hexane is non-polar and is not attracted strongly enough to the ions.
The ions already exist in the solid lattice; water does not create them. Water dissolves NaCl because its polar molecules are attracted to the existing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

mcqs.q: Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, Cs⁺ 167, Ca²⁺ 100, Ba²⁺ 135, F⁻ 133, O²⁻ 140, S²⁻ 184. Which compound has the largest lattice enthalpy?
options: NaF
CsF
BaS
CaO
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: Lattice enthalpy increases with ion charge and decreases with ion radius. CaO and BaS contain 2+ and 2− ions, which attract far more strongly than the 1+ and 1− ions of NaF and CsF. Of the two, CaO has the smaller ions (sum of radii 240 pm against 319 pm), so its lattice enthalpy is the largest.
rationales: NaF does have the smallest sum of ionic radii (235 pm), but its ions are only singly charged. CaO's 2+ and 2− ions attract far more strongly, and a 5 pm difference in radii cannot make up for that.

CsF has the largest electronegativity difference, but lattice enthalpy depends on the charges and radii of the ions. Cs⁺ is the largest cation here (167 pm) and both ions are singly charged, so CsF's lattice enthalpy is much smaller than CaO's.

BaS has the largest ions here (sum of radii 319 pm). Larger ions attract each other less strongly because their centres are further apart, so BaS has a smaller lattice enthalpy than CaO, whose ions carry the same charges.

Lattice enthalpy increases with ion charge and decreases with ion radius. CaO and BaS contain 2+ and 2− ions, which attract far more strongly than the 1+ and 1− ions of NaF and CsF. Of the two, CaO has the smaller ions (sum of radii 240 pm against 319 pm), so its lattice enthalpy is the largest.

mcqs.q: Lattice enthalpy is a measure of the strength of the ionic bonding in a compound. Ionic radii (pm): Na⁺ 102, K⁺ 138, F⁻ 133, Cl⁻ 181. Which shows the lattice enthalpies of NaF, NaCl and KCl in decreasing order?
options: KCl > NaCl > NaF
NaF > NaCl > KCl
NaF > KCl > NaCl
NaF = NaCl = KCl
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: All three compounds contain 1+ and 1− ions, so the radii decide. The sums of the radii are NaF 235 pm, NaCl 283 pm and KCl 319 pm; the closer the ion centres, the stronger the attraction, so NaF > NaCl > KCl.
rationales: This is the reverse order. Larger ions have their centres further apart, so they attract each other less strongly: KCl, with the largest ions, has the smallest lattice enthalpy.

All three compounds contain 1+ and 1− ions, so the radii decide. The sums of the radii are NaF 235 pm, NaCl 283 pm and KCl 319 pm; the closer the ion centres, the stronger the attraction, so NaF > NaCl > KCl.

This follows the electronegativity difference, which is larger for K–Cl than for Na–Cl. Lattice enthalpy depends on the charges and radii of the ions; KCl has larger ions than NaCl, so its lattice enthalpy is smaller.
The charges are the same, but lattice enthalpy also depends on ion radius. The sums of the radii differ (235, 283 and 319 pm), so the lattice enthalpies differ, decreasing as the ions get larger.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride has a very low volatility: it does not evaporate at room temperature and melts only at 801 °C. Which explanation is correct?
options: Every ion is strongly attracted to many ions of opposite charge.
Its particles are so heavy that they cannot move fast enough to escape.
Evaporating it would break the strong bond in every NaCl molecule.
Sodium is a metal with a high boiling point, and NaCl keeps this property.
mcqs.specStatementText: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
mcqs.explain: In the lattice every ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge and attracted to all of them. Separating the ions means overcoming many strong electrostatic attractions, which needs a large amount of energy, so sodium chloride has a low volatility.
rationales: In the lattice every ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge and attracted to all of them. Separating the ions means overcoming many strong electrostatic attractions, which needs a large amount of energy, so sodium chloride has a low volatility.

Sodium chloride's relative formula mass, M_r, is only 58.44, lower than that of many volatile liquids such as octane (114.26). Its low volatility comes from the strong attractions between its ions, not from mass.

Solid sodium chloride contains no molecules. It is a lattice in which each ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it, and these attractions must be overcome to melt or vaporize it.
A compound does not keep the properties of its elements: sodium chloride is not a metal. Its low volatility comes from its own structure, a lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic attractions.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the formula of an ionic compound is correct?
options: Ammonium hydrogencarbonate has the chemical formula (NH₄)₂HCO₃
Aluminium phosphate has the chemical formula Al₂(PO₄)₃
Ammonium carbonate has the chemical formula (NH₄)₂CO₃
Potassium phosphate has the chemical formula KPO₄
mcqs.specStatementText: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
mcqs.explain: Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Two NH₄⁺ ions (+2) balance one CO₃²⁻ ion (−2), and the ammonium ion is kept intact and bracketed.
rationales: Hydrogencarbonate is HCO₃⁻: adding H⁺ to CO₃²⁻ changes the charge from 2− to 1−. One NH₄⁺ balances one HCO₃⁻, so ammonium hydrogencarbonate is NH₄HCO₃.
Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, not PO₄²⁻: the -ate ending does not fix the charge. Al³⁺ and PO₄³⁻ combine 1 : 1, so aluminium phosphate is AlPO₄.
Ammonium is NH₄⁺ and carbonate is CO₃²⁻. Two NH₄⁺ ions (+2) balance one CO₃²⁻ ion (−2), and the ammonium ion is kept intact and bracketed.
One K⁺ (+1) and one PO₄³⁻ (−3) give a total charge of −2, so KPO₄ is not neutral. Three K⁺ ions balance one PO₄³⁻ ion: K₃PO₄.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Chemistry (guide first assessment 2025); topic S2.1 The ionic model

specStatements.text: When metal atoms lose electrons, they form positive ions called cations. When non-metal atoms gain electrons, they form negative ions called anions.
specStatements.guidance: Predict the charge of an ion from the electron configuration of the atom. The formation of ions with different charges from a transition element should be included.

specStatements.text: The ionic bond is formed by electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
specStatements.guidance: Deduce the formula and name of an ionic compound from its component ions, including polyatomic ions. Binary ionic compounds are named with the cation first, followed by the anion. The anion adopts the suffix “ide”. Interconvert names and formulas of binary ionic compounds. The following polyatomic ions should be known by name and formula: ammonium NH₄⁺, hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, hydrogencarbonate HCO₃⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, phosphate PO₄³⁻.

specStatements.text: Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures, represented by empirical formulas.
specStatements.guidance: Explain the physical properties of ionic compounds to include volatility, electrical conductivity and solubility. Include lattice enthalpy as a measure of the strength of the ionic bond in different compounds, influenced by ion radius and charge.

scopeNotes.statement: The formation of ions with different charges from a transition element should be included.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Iron (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, q03) and copper (Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺, q02, q07) are the transition-element examples, tested through electron configurations (q02, q03) and through formulas with names (q07). The explanation of variable oxidation states through closely spaced successive ionization energies is HL content (S3.1.9) and is not used on these SL statements.

scopeNotes.statement: Include lattice enthalpy as a measure of the strength of the ionic bond in different compounds, influenced by ion radius and charge.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Lattice enthalpy is defined (c14) and compared qualitatively from ion charges and given ionic radii (q13, q14). No Born–Haber cycle (HL, R1.2.5) and no lattice-enthalpy calculation appears, and no numerical lattice enthalpy value is quoted anywhere in the topic.
